opus-5.5.text:
That's a good way to frame it, and honestly I didn't plan it as a thread at the beginning. It's more something I noticed looking back.

When I started, during my PhD, the question was how to build the right inductive biases into a model. With holistically-nested edge detection, the idea was that a deep network should learn at multiple scales, and you should supervise it at multiple levels, because that's how visual structure works. Then ResNeXt was about the architecture itself: is there a simple, repeatable structure, like grouped transformations, that gives you a better representation without hand-engineering every layer? So early on, the "structural prior" was very literal. It lived in the network design.

Over time my view shifted. The field moved toward the idea that maybe we don't need strong priors, that with enough data and compute, a generic architecture like a Transformer learns everything. I think that's partly true, but not the whole story. ConvNeXt was a reaction to that. We asked: if you modernize a ConvNet with all the training recipes Transformers enjoy, how much of the gap is really about architecture, and how much is everything else? The answer was that convolution's priors, locality and translation equivariance, were still very competitive. So the priors weren't wrong. They had been confounded with other factors.

Then there's the self-supervised side, with MoCo-style contrastive learning and masked autoencoders. There the prior moves out of the architecture and into the objective. What do you ask the model to predict? What invariances do you encourage? Masking images and reconstructing them assumes something about visual signals: they're highly redundant, so you need to mask aggressively to force real understanding. That's a structural prior too, just expressed through the learning task.

And more recently, with diffusion Transformers and our work on multimodal models like Cambrian, I see the same question again from another angle. In generation, people sometimes think the representation and the generative model are separate problems. I don't think so. Good generation needs good representation, and you can make generative models learn much faster by aligning them with strong visual representations. In multimodal LLMs, I've found the vision part is often the weakest link. People plug in an encoder and assume language will handle the rest. But if the visual representation is poor, no amount of language modeling saves you.

So, if I had to summarize the thread: I keep asking where the structure should live. In the architecture, the objective, the data, or the interaction between modalities? The answer keeps moving, but I don't believe in a completely structure-free learner. The world has structure, especially the visual world, and the art is deciding which structure to bake in and which to let the model discover. That tension has been the most interesting part of my research, and I think it matters even more now as we think about world models and grounding intelligence in the physical world, beyond text.

r001.rationale: The response frames where structure should live as an ongoing question and says the answer keeps moving, conveying that representation learning with structural priors remains unresolved.

r002.rationale: The response says the research thread was noticed in retrospect, but does not present fragmentation in the PhD trajectory as an unavoidable consequence of pursuing representation learning as an overarching topic.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I look back, I don't think I ever sat down and decided "structural priors" would be my theme. It emerged in hindsight. But if you line the work up, there is a pretty consistent question underneath: what should we build into a model by hand, and what should we let the data teach it?

Early on, during my PhD with Zhuowen Tu, I was deeply influenced by the way vision researchers thought about structure. Edges, boundaries, hierarchies. Holistically-nested edge detection was about using a deep network to recover a very classical kind of structure, the contours of the world, and we had to think carefully about how multi-scale supervision shapes what the intermediate layers learn. That was really a lesson that architecture is a prior. Where you put the skip connections, where you attach the losses, those choices encode beliefs about the visual world.

ResNeXt pushed that further. People remember it as "grouped convolutions," but the real idea for me was the cardinality dimension. We were asking, what is the right unit of computation? Instead of only going deeper or wider, we aggregated many simple transformations, and that structural choice turned out to be a surprisingly good inductive bias. It was also my first strong experience of a principle that stayed with me: a simple, clean, repeatable design often beats something intricate.

Then there was a long stretch where the field moved toward self-supervision, and I spent a lot of time thinking about how priors should live in the pretext task rather than the architecture. Contrastive learning is a kind of prior about invariance. Masked autoencoding is a prior about redundancy in natural signals. So the structure moved out of the network diagram and into the objective, but it is the same question in a different place.

ConvNeXt was almost a reaction to the Transformer moment. Everyone was saying the attention mechanism was what mattered. I wanted to test that. If you take a ConvNet and modernize the design decisions, the macro design, the training recipe, the normalization, how much of the gap closes? It turned out most of it. That told me that a lot of what we attribute to a specific operator is really about the surrounding structure and the recipe. Convolution is a strong spatial prior, attention is a weaker one, and which is better depends on how much data you have and what you want to transfer.

And now, with diffusion transformers and more recently with things like representation alignment, the question has turned toward generative models. A diffusion model is implicitly learning a representation, but it is not necessarily learning a good one. So we started asking, can a strong discriminative representation act as a structural prior for generation? That turned out to be a very productive direction, and it closes a loop for me, because the generative model is now being guided by exactly the kind of representation I spent the earlier years trying to learn.

So the thread is something like this. Scale and data are extraordinary, but they are not free. Every architecture, every objective, is quietly a hypothesis about the structure of the world. I have spent my career trying to make those hypotheses explicit, test them honestly, and keep only the ones that survive. Sometimes the answer is "add more structure," sometimes it is "remove structure and let the data speak." The interesting science is in knowing which situation you are in.

r001.rationale: The response describes a continuing research question and evolving approaches, but does not clearly state that representation learning with structural priors remains an incompletely solved problem.

r002.rationale: The response describes the PhD work as part of a consistent thread in hindsight. It does not present fragmentation in the PhD trajectory as unavoidable or connect it to pursuing representation learning as an overarching topic.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a useful way to connect the questions I’m interested in: how much structure should we put into a model, and how much should we let it learn from data?

Representation learning can sound like we’re asking the model to discover everything by itself. But we always make choices about architecture, objectives, and how we present the data. Those choices introduce priors. They influence which relationships are easy for the model to capture and which are difficult.

The interesting part, for me, is that the right balance can change. A structural constraint might help learning when data or computation is limited, but it might also become a restriction as we scale. So I wouldn’t frame the goal as finding one architecture or one prior that works forever. It’s understanding what a particular structure contributes, and whether we still need it under different conditions.

That’s the thread I’d emphasize: using structure to support learning, while continually questioning which assumptions should remain explicit and which can be learned.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the changing balance of structure and learning, but does not clearly state that representation learning with structural priors remains an incompletely solved research problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the recurring question is: what structure should we build into a model, and what should we let it learn from data? Representation learning can sound like we want to learn everything from scratch, but we always make choices about architecture, objectives, and the data itself. Those choices introduce priors.

The useful prior is one that makes learning easier without limiting what the model can discover. Structure can encourage a model to reuse features, combine information across scales, or organize computation more effectively. But we should also be willing to question that structure as our data and computational resources change. Something that helps in one setting can become a constraint in another.

So I see a consistent thread, but not necessarily a commitment to one particular architecture. It’s more a way of approaching the problem: introduce structure, understand why it helps, and then ask whether it is still necessary. The goal is to find the right relationship between what we design and what the representation learns.
